p.i: In the name of the Lord, let us act and prevail.

book.p: Here begins the order of the six principles of faith, by our master and teacher, our diadem, our crowning garland, our glorious adorning headdress, our magnificence, the distinguished sage, revealer of secrets and profundities, the honorable R. Israel the Judge (ha-dayyan), son of the honorable, great and saintly one who appointed Wisdom and Discernment as his nurse, noble and honored in Israel, our master and teacher Samuel the Judge (ha-dayyan) ha-Ma^^^^02bfaravi, may his soul be bound up in the bond of life (1 Samuel 25:29). Amen, Neṣaḥ, Selah; and peace upon all Israel.
The First Tenet

p.i: Belief in Divinity

book.p: Every Israelite must believe that God possesses complete knowledge1 of the heavens and all that is in them, of the earth and all that is upon it, of the seas and their inhabitants, of the mountains and their valleys. Sole Creator, exceedingly majestic, with neither beginning nor end. He can neither be overpowered, nor conquered; He has no upper limit that might set Him below, nor a lower limit that might set Him above; He has no flanks that might contain Him, nor sides that might delimit Him. Whatever He wills to be, comes to be; His Oneness is timeless and placeless; He brought all that exists into being from nothing, timelessly remaining separate from them. He lives and does not die, endures and does not perish; He is self-sufficient and not in need, generous and not miserly, wise and not ignorant. His knowledge encompasses all things past, present, and future. All creatures depend upon Him, and place their trust in His sufficiency. He does not become many with the multiplication of His attributes; He neither grows nor shrinks in His essence; He is imperceptible to the five senses, transcending both taste and touch. Let it not be said that He is an accident or a substance, that He disappears or that He appears to the senses, that He slumbers or that He wakes, that He may be overpowered or conquered, or that He is a body or a power in a body. His name is “God” (allāh); no name is mightier than His. Obedience does not benefit Him, and sin does not harm Him. He hears all prayer, accepts repentance, supports those who stumble, dispels grief, delivers from ruin, forgives sin, is faithful to promises, keeps His covenant; Bestower, Compassionate One, Ruler, Judge, Most Merciful of All; who takes up the claim of the oppressed against the oppressors; who requites the steadfast and those who suffer. There is not a trace of injustice in His judgments; His commandments and prohibitions are untainted by corruption. He puts to death and gives life, brings illness and heals, allots poverty and wealth. There is no god other than Him, His Sublime Highness and Perfect Majesty, to whom all foreheads bow, of whom all mouths speak in praise and exaltation. There is no favor but His favor.

May His most great name be blessed, sanctified, praised, glorified, esteemed, extolled above all else, delighted in, declared mighty and sublime, and exalted forever and ever! We ask Him (may He be praised and exalted) to safeguard us from offense and error in this world, and in [matters of] religion; and let Him not consider us among the unbelievers.

p.i: Amen, Amen, and praise be to God, the Lord of Worlds.

book.p: The Second Tenet

p.i: Belief in Messengership

book.p: One must believe that the most perfect specimen of humanity with respect to moral dispositions, intellect, mind, judgment, dignity, humility, eminence, and nobility was the illustrious and noble and venerated master; the exemplar of all prophets and messengers, leader of the ancients and moderns, concerning whom all those who profess religion (al-milliyyīn) have concurred, affirming the soundness of his true message, declaring his messages to be true, and upholding his miracles. All of the prophets have testified that he spoke with the Lord Almighty, and that his Lord summoned him, entrusting him into His confidence in the uppermost heavens. Among his miracles: he turned the staff into a snake, and back (Exodus 4:3–4); he turned his hand white, and back (Exodus 4:6–7); the proofs and signs that he produced with the ten quaking plagues, smiting Pharaoh (Exodus 7–12); then he parted the raging sea (Exodus 14:16–28); he brought waves of flowing water forth from the rock (Exodus 17:5–7); he healed affliction;1 he brought down manna and quail [from the sky] (Exodus 16:1–36); by lifting his hands, he defeated tyrants (Exodus 17:8–13); by his glory, conquering kings were brought low (Numbers 21:21–35); he addressed [the Israelites] on Mount Sinai (cf. Exodus 20:16); his noble face was illuminated with godly light (Exodus 34:29–30); he received two inscribed tablets from the Heavenly Host, containing a hidden jewel, inscribed with the word of God (Exodus 31:18); an intercessor, who interceded on behalf of recalcitrant sinners (Exodus 32:11–14); he watched the processions of the Holy Regent, coming and going. He exceeds all of the other prophets in might and nobility, as the sun outshines the setting moon; for he is their full moon and their commander (badruhum wa-ṣadruhum), their authority revolves around him. He is our master, our exemplar, our leader, the crown of our head, the pillar of our tent, our intercessor before the One whom we worship, possessor of our Law, Moses the Spokesman, the son of Amram (mūsā al-kalīm ibn ^^^^02bfimrān). May God Most High's peace be upon him, and upon his noble predecessors—gratifying peace until the Day of Judgment.

p.i: Praise be to God, the Lord of Worlds, Amen.

book.p: The Third Tenet

p.i: Belief in the Prophets and Messengers Who Came Before

book.p: [Moses], at the Same Time as He Did, and After Him

This is the belief in those of whose reliable prophecy the True Books speak. This is the case concerning those preceding Moses, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (peace be upon them), concerning whom it has been said, Do not touch My anointed ones; do not harm My prophets (1 Chronicles 16:22). Among his contemporaries were Aaron, Eleazar, Phineas, Joshua, and the seventy elders (peace be upon them). Among those following him were such figures as Samuel the Rama^^^^00adthite, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel and his companions (peace be upon them). [These are the prophets] for whose sake miracles occurred, and through whom demonstrations, proofs, and signs came to pass, such as the halting of the sun and moon for Joshua (Joshua 10:12), and the elimination of the plague by Aaron, using his fire-pan (Numbers 17:11). Elijah walked between the [parted] waters (2 Kings 2:14), caused fire to descend from heaven (ibid., 1:12), resuscitated the Zarephathite woman's son (1 Kings 17:9,17–24), caused rain to pour from heaven by his supplication (1 Kings 17:1,18:1), and brought blessings upon those who hosted him. Elisha (peace be upon him) also walked between the [parted] waters (2 Kings 2:14), made an axe head float (2 Kings 6:1–7), and resuscitated the Shunammite woman's son (2 Kings 4:8,12,18–37). This includes the signs and proofs that are particular to each and every one of the prophets, a full account of which would be too lengthy. Their truth has been transmitted, unafflicted by doubt or dispute. Each modeled the Law (sharī^^^^02bfa) of Moses, son of Amram, father of the prophets, fulfilling and affirming it, acquiring knowledge and acting (^^^^02bfālimīn wa-^^^^02bfāmilīn) in accordance with it. None innovated any new law, religion, or belief; indeed, their sincerity is well established. God's peace be upon them all.

p.i: Amen, and praise be to God, the Lord of Worlds, Amen.

book.p: The Fourth Tenet

p.i: Belief in the Message

book.p: One must believe that the pure, sacred, and sublime Law, which is called the Torah—may God magnify and glorify it in the hearts of all the creatures, as the prophet proclaimed, The Lord desires His [servant's] vindication, that he may magnify and glorify his Torah (Isaiah 42:21)—is that which was dictated to our faithful master Moses (peace be upon him) by the Heavenly Host, without any intermediary: word by word, letter for letter, accurately recording the letters and discourse; eloquent, pure, sullied by neither contradiction nor doubt, sheer truth; a perfect Law, with just decrees; for all eternity, it will never be abrogated nor annulled; its transmission ensured by the unbroken succession of reports, its correctness ensured throughout the ages. It is comprised of five books. Intellects have affirmed their content and deemed them true. All those who profess religion (al-milliyyīn) have heard its decrees and extolled them. From its exalted station, it informed us concerning the permissibility of slaughtering animals, attesting to the noble wisdom of the Permitter, surpassing the wisdom that can be comprehended by intellects and minds in its demonstrable justness, and the wisdom of the One who affects its application. No book is comparable to it; none gifted with an understanding heart can oppose it. As He said (glory be to Him) concerning it, No weapon formed against you shall succeed, and every tongue that contends with you at law you shall defeat. Such is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord, such their triumph through Me—declares the Lord (Isaiah 54:17).
The Fifth Tenet
Belief in the [Holy] Site (Qibla)

One must believe that the sacred, noble, and venerated site1 (qibla)—may God restore it to its honor, dignity, and majesty—is the place chosen from among all others, so that the venerated light of the Divine Presence (shekhinah) might dwell within it. As He (may He be exalted) proclaimed to Solomon (peace be upon him), Now I have chosen and consecrated this House that My name be there forever. My eyes and my heart shall always be there (2 Chronicles 7:16). It is our duty to orient ourselves toward that place in prayer, facing it during worshipful acts [such as] slaughtering and circumcision. We orient even our deceased toward it, both when they are above the ground and beneath it. This is the place of which it is said, Even unto His habitation shall you seek, and there you are to go (Deuteronomy 12:5). This is the place to which all the nations will come to pray, as He said (glory be to Him), For My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7).
The Sixth Tenet

p.i: Belief in the Day of Judgment

book.p: This means that one must believe that the Appointed Time1 is inevitable. This is when the dead will be restored to their former living state, as their souls are returned to them, and they are resurrected from their graves and returned to the face of the Earth, and their bodies are restored to their former state—whether from the bottom of the sea, or from caves and dark valleys, just as The Lord said, `I will retrieve from Bashan, I will retrieve from the depths of the sea…' (Psalms 68:23). [It is the time at which] each and every one of them will receive their just deserts, altogether, [for acts committed] in secret,2 for all of one's obedient and rebellious deeds. All of one's actions are unfurled in God's presence, the good weighed against the bad. Those whose deeds are righteous shall be transported to the abode of bliss, and shall be granted the great triumph that souls desire, in unceasing and perpetual conjunction with splendor and glory.

But woe to the those whose deeds are unrighteous, who shall be taken to the abode of punishment, to humiliation and feebleness, and long-lasting suffering. There they shall be consigned unbearable misery and suffering that cannot be borne for all of eternity, without respite. As He said concerning the wicked, Their worms shall not die, nor their fire be quenched; they shall be a horror to all flesh (Isaiah 66:24). But of the righteous He said, You shall come to see the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve Him (Malachi 3:18).
Therefore, we ask God for forgiveness, health, compassion, atonement, and well-being in this world and in the Hereafter.

p.i: Amen, and Peace. Here end the Six Tenets. Peace.

book.p: The Regulations of Slaughter
In the name of the Lord, God of the World1 (Gen. 21:33),
blessed be His name.

The Regulations of Slaughter by our master and teacher, the sage, great among God's people, the honorable R. Israel the Judge, indicated and mentioned above, may he rest in Eden, [and] may his soul be bound up in the bond of life (1 Samuel 25:29). Amen, Neṣaḥ, Selah, and Peace.
Discourse on Slaughter

Among its subjects are (i) regulations of the slaughterer, (ii) the slaughtered [animal], (iii) the instrument, (iv) how [the instrument] must be used, (v) the site of slaughtering, (vi) what must be cut, (vii) what must not be cut, (viii) how [the animal] should be handled, (ix) the blessing [to be recited], and (x) what must be done following slaughter. In total, it comes to ten chapters.
Chapter I

p.i: Regulations of the Slaughterer

book.p: The slaughterer must be an intelligent and reasonable adult, strong-spirited and insightful;1 who openly follows the Law of Moses, father of all of the prophets, peace be upon him, and who repudiates any opinion that is incompatible with it; a person of good conduct, who regularly performs prayers; who rarely makes oaths or jests; who is dependable and honest in interpersonal conduct; who is pious and virtuous; who believes that there is recompense for the slaughtered animal, even though he does not know what it is; who is knowledgeable in what is permitted and what is forbidden, and in the regulations that render eating the animal permissible.
Chapter II
Regulations of [the Animal That Is to Be] Slaughtered

If it is a wild or domesticated [land] animal, it must have split hooves and chew its cud. According to Jewish opinion, a mother and its young may not be slaughtered on the same day; if its father is known, the same rule applies. The [animal to be] slaughtered must be over seven days old, and there must not be any doubt; it cannot be pregnant, sick, injured, or attacked by a predator; and there should be no [reason to] fear that it is near to its death.

If it is a bird, there must be an undisputed tradition among the Jews regarding its acceptability, permissibility, and identification; they must be in possession of a sound tradition, excluding the inspection of its characteristics. [Such permitted species] include doves, pigeons, chickens, geese, partridges, wild quail, and common quail.
If there is a doubt regarding any animal's status—in the characteristics for a land animal, or in the tradition for a bird—it may not be slaughtered.
As with [land] animals, only birds that are of sound body may be slaughtered.
Chapter III

p.i: Regulations of the Instrument

book.p: The instrument used for the act of slaughter must be longer than the width of the animal's neck, so that its head will not enter [into the animal's neck] when it is drawn [along it], nor stick [into the animal's neck] when brought back over the [animal's] skin. It should have enough thickness and solidity1 that it will not bend or quiver, so it can be used for slaughtering. It should not have any curvature, nicks, or coarseness; it must follow a straight line, cut deeply, and be as sharp as possible. It may not be [made from] glass, ceramic, wood, bone, reed, or a claw, for one cannot be sure that they will not break or blunt when drawn over the [animal's] skin. [The instrument] should be made from iron so that the slaughtering process will be reliable, because iron is stronger than the aforementioned materials.
Chapter IV
How the Slaughterer Must Use [the Instrument]

p.i: When He Wants to Slaughter

book.p: One must draw the blade over the neck underneath the cricoid cartilage, back and forth1 with its sharp edge without stabbing or prodding, for such things increase the pain of the slaughtered animal. One should not chop or press, because the slaughterer cannot retain full control in such a fashion. The motion should be continuous, without slowing, without lifting the hand, and without even momentary weakness, for any such motion due to slowing or lifting one's hand would constitute a second act of slaughter. One must first cut the most anterior part of the neck and then the jugular veins on either side.
Chapter V

p.i: On the Site of Slaughtering

book.p: [The location at which the throat is to be cut] is at the front rather than the back of the neck, and close to the head rather than far from it, so that if one grabs the throat,1 the jugular veins will not rotate with it; for when one grips them from their point of origin they are not slack, enabling one to cut them. We know that “slaughtering” (dhabīḥa) is [a term that refers specifically to cutting] of the neck, for the Hebrew and Arabic terms are cognate: zeviḥah [in Hebrew] and dhabīḥa [in Arabic]. If one were to say, “So-and-so has been wounded,” the listener would reply, “Where on his body?” Similarly, if one were to say, “So-and-so has been hit,” the listener would reply, “Where?” But if one were to say, “So-and-so has been slaughtered (dhubiḥa),” this plainly refers to the neck, without any further question. Therefore, when the verse states, You may slaughter (tizbaḥ) and eat meat (Deuteronomy 12:15), and, You shall slaughter (ve-zavaḥta) any of your cattle or sheep (ibid., 12:21), we know with certainty that this refers to the neck.
Chapter VI

p.i: On What Must Be Cut

book.p: These are what must be cut in the neck of an animal: the esophagus (for food), the trachea (for breathing), and the two jugular veins (the locus of the blood). By cutting these, slaughter is regarded as valid by all Jews. The same is true if any one of them is partially, rather than fully, severed (?). However, as long as one of the jugular veins remains [intact], none consider this to be [valid] slaughter. This is one of our [Karaite?] arguments.1 Whatever skin, flesh, or veins are cut during slaughtering do not invalidate the animal, because what must be cut can only be accessed through them; necessity thus dictates that they must be cut. By cutting the aforementioned [parts of the throat, the animal] dies and bleeds out faster than if one cut anything else.
Chapter VII

p.i: On What Must Not Be Cut

book.p: While he draws the knife [along the animal's throat], the slaughterer must be careful not to break any bone or to cut so deeply that he reaches the spinal marrow; indeed, not paying attention, one might sever the head from the animal's body. It would then not convulse, its blood would remain within it, and it would be rendered impermissible (ḥarām). For we must be punctilious in refraining from the consumption of blood. If the blood from slaughtering does not pour out while the animal is convulsing, salting [the meat] will not extract it. The proof of this is that the meat of the neck cannot be cleansed by salting, due to the blood spilled over it while [the animal is being] slaughtered. As the verse states, For the blood is the life, and you must not consume the life with the flesh (Deuteronomy 12:23).
Chapter VIII

p.i: How the Animal That Is to Be Slaughtered Should Be Restrained

book.p: The person restraining the animal should be somebody other than the slaughterer, whether it is large or small. The slaughterer should position his hand on the neck that is to be cut, push the cricoid cartilage rostrally, grip the animal's throat and the adjacent part in the front, and reach under and cut the throat. One should face in the direction of the sacred site (al-qibla al-quddūsiyya) [i.e., Jerusalem], representing the sacrifices that were offered [in the Temple]. As it is stated, He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar, before the Lord (Leviticus 1:11).

If it is a bird, one should hold its wings in one hand, lift its legs between his fingers (namely, the little finger and the adjacent one), and hold its breast upright so that its back lies on the slaughterer's palm. One should then pull its head, place one's fingers on its neck so that it sticks out its tongue, and then grip the throat by the skin so that it cannot swallow (lest the tongue or cricoid cartilage be cut, which would render it impermissible). If it is a large bird, then the slaughterer should place its wings under his legs. He may then position himself, and cut the throat.

If, due to its strength, an animal must be bound while it is handled, then let it be bound; and let it not be freed, and let it remain bound, until the slaughter is completed. But afterwards, it should be untied so that the animal might not be prevented from convulsing, which would prevent the blood from pouring out.
Chapter IX

p.i: On the Blessing

book.p: We should preface all of our actions by mentioning our Lord, and we should not make use of anything that God (may He be exalted) has bestowed upon us until we have offered thanks to Him. As Solomon (peace be upon him) said, In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths smooth (Proverbs 3:6). For He brought us into existence out of nothing, dealt favorably with us, appointed us as rulers over all creatures, and permitted us to make use of whatever we can in the temporal realm. As David (peace be upon him) said, You have made him master over Your handiwork, laying the world at his feet, sheep and oxen, all of them… the birds of the heavens, the fish of the sea… (Psalms 8:7–9).

And so, we should thank Him for the permission that He has given us to make use of anything that we know to be proper from the perspective of both our religious and worldly existence. Thus, whenever we approach the act of slaughtering any animal, we make the blessing, “Blessed are You, Lord our God, the King of the Universe, Who permitted us to slaughter pure animals”—that is for a species of [land] animal. For a bird, we conclude it with [the expression] “pure birds.” We may then slaughter it. <If the slaughterer neglects to make the blessing, no harm is done; let him return to the slaughtered animal [to recite it]. Similarly,> if the slaughterer neglects [to face the sacred] site (qibla) [i.e., Jerusalem], this does not have any effect on [the permissibility of] the animal. A single blessing is sufficient for even a million animals, as long as they are slaughtered consecutively. However, if the slaughterer makes an interruption and then returns, he must recite a second blessing.
Chapter X

p.i: On What Must Be Done After Slaughter

book.p: It is incumbent upon every Israelite not to increase the suffering of the animal beyond the suffering endured during slaughter. To this end, as we have seen, we are careful not to demean the animal during the act of slaughter itself, having observed the compassion of our Lord (may His majesty be exalted!). As David (peace be upon him) stated, His mercy is upon all His works (Psalms 145:9); and we see that it is stated, You shall not take the mother together with her young (Deuteronomy 22:6); and also, You shall not slaughter it with its young on the same day (Leviticus 22:28); and also, You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk (Exodus 23:19).

We thus walk in the ways of our Lord, and we stipulate that the slaughterer must be a believer, so that the compassion of faith will be in his heart, and so that he will not act cruelly by making any unnecessary cut during the slaughter. Everything prescribed concerning the animal to be slaughtered is for the sake of compassion. For any non-permitted slaughter would be a waste and an offense, since we would be unable to benefit from it. Similarly, if the animal is sick or injured, we should not add further suffering [based on the principle], it with its young (Leviticus 22:28). A pregnant animal is also considered “it with its young.” Moreover, [this principle is related to the other laws of slaughter], just as we are punctilious concerning the instrument, the cutting motion, and the cut—all for the sake of compassion. If the process that renders the consumption of meat permissible has taken place, [this means that] the slaughterer has not been excessively harsh as long as the animal's spirit clings to its body. If all of this comes to pass, it only remains to us to use [the animal], just as we use minerals and plants, in terms of dividing it up. We must not make use of any slaughtered animal until it has stopped moving.

In the case of birds and hunted animals (Leviticus 17:13),1 we must cover their blood with earth—real and not figurative [earth]—all over. One should only slaughter if one has earth.2 While covering [the blood], one should recite the blessing: “Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Who has sanctified us with His commandments, and commanded us concerning covering the blood with earth.” If it is unclear whether a [land] animal is domesticated or wild, its blood must be covered with earth when it is slaughtered. Its fat is forbidden.

If one forgets to cover [an animal's] blood, [the meat] is not forbidden [for consumption]. If one inadvertently slaughters it with its young (Leviticus 22:28), it is not forbidden. But if they are cooked together, [the meat] is forbidden, by analogy with [the commandment], You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk (Exodus 23:19).

p.i: The Ten Chapters are complete. Peace upon all Israel.

book.p: In the name of the Lord, God of the World (Gen. 21:33),
blessed be His name.
A Discourse on Factors That Invalidate Slaughter
There are five things that invalidate an act of slaughter:
1. Shehiyyah, meaning “slowing down”; [this term is derived] from [the Biblical usage], The man stood gazing in wonderment1 (mishta^^^^02beeh) at her (Genesis 24:21).
2. Derasah, meaning “chopping or pressing” on the site.
3. Hagramah, meaning “cutting the upper throat or lopping”; from, [Her judges are wolves of the steppe,] they break not a bone (garmu)2 for the morning (Zephaniah 3:3).
4. Ḥaladah, meaning “concealing”; from, [You have made my life just handbreadths long;] if I vanish (ḥeldi),3 is as nothing in Your sight (Psalms 39:6).
5. ^^^^02bfIqqur, meaning “tearing”; from, and a time to uproot (la^^^^02bfaqor) [that which is planted] (Ecclesiastes 3:2).

These five things have been transmitted among all Israelites as a continuous, undisputed tradition, attaining a consensus on these five aforementioned terms. As for the interpretation of each term, the soundest method in [establishing their meaning] is that which conforms to analysis (al-naẓar), as discussed by the Sages (peace be upon them).

Concerning the interpretation of shehiyyah (i.e., slowing down): it is when something startles the slaughterer or hinders him from completing the act of slaughter, so that he lifts his hand with the knife, from the animal's neck. [In such a case, the slaughterer] must not resume [the act]. Rather, he must investigate whether what he has already cut suffices, or whether the animal is forbidden [for consumption].

Concerning the interpretation of derasah (i.e., chopping or pressing): it is when the slaughterer places the knife on the slaughtered [animal's] neck and presses down with his hand as if he were cutting a solid object, such as cheese. Or, if one strikes the neck with the blade, just as a butcher hacks with a cleaver in order to break a bone. These two actions are forbidden and invalidate the slaughter.

Concerning the interpretation of ḥaladah (i.e., concealing): it is when something covers the knife, so that the slaughterer cannot watch it pass over the neck, or when the top of the knife is so narrow that it accidentally slips under the [four] signs (simanim) or between the esophagus and the trachea. This is not considered slaughtering, and the slaughterer is not permitted to turn the blade around and slaughter.

Concerning the interpretation of hagramah (i.e., cutting the upper throat or lopping): it is when the cut is made in the cricoid cartilage or above it. This typically occurs when the slaughterer is careless when pushing [the cartilage] rostrally, and the slaughtered [animal] swallows without the slaughterer noticing, and grips something other than the esophagus and trachea. The cut is then made at the wrong site, and the [animal] becomes forbidden. This also occurs when the slaughterer cuts in a lopping or diagonal fashion, as he might miss the trachea and cut into or above the cricoid cartilage, rendering the animal forbidden. Only the four signs (simanim) should be cut.

Concerning the interpretation of ^^^^02bfiqqur (i.e., tearing): it is when the signs (simanim) are “torn” from their place before they are cut. This may happen in two ways: one caused by the slaughterer, and the other caused by the slaughtered [animal]. It may be caused by the slaughterer, if he pulls the signs (simanim) forcefully and tears them from their place. Or it may be caused by the slaughtered [animal], if while it is being positioned for slaughtering, it struggles with its neck in order to free itself, tearing the signs (simanim).

The slaughterer should therefore be vigilant in all that has been discussed, as well as in this matter, considering whether the slaughtered [animal's] throat is intact before the act of slaughter. Likewise, he should inspect it for injuries or anything obstructing its passages that would prevent it from being slaughtered. Likewise, he should be vigilant in examining his instrument before and after anybody slaughters with it, so that the slaughtering will be valid. For one cannot be sure that it has not developed a nick or some other kind of hindrance.

A slaughterer must not slaughter a second [animal] without first inspecting the first animal, so that his [second] slaughter will not be disqualified. One must not slaughter [another animal] with the knife that one already used until one has washed it, at the very least in order to cleanse it of the blood of an [animal] killed impermissibly (ṭerefah), so that he does not ruin the next [animal to be] slaughtered.

All of these matters depend on the integrity of the slaughterer. If he fears God (may He be exalted), he will be delivered from doom in both realms. For he is duty-bound to others, who place their confidence in him that he will not give them anything forbidden to eat. In this world, he must strive to redeem his soul, so that he will escape punishment and torment, and be granted bounty in this world and reward in the Hereafter. Let the True One (may He be praised and exalted) help him and assist him, for He knows his intent, and He (may He be praised and exalted) is his Guide toward what is right.

p.i: May His name be blessed and His praise exalted.
Amen, Neṣaḥ, Selah.

book.p: In the name of the Lord, God of the World (Gen. 21:33),
blessed be His name.
A Chapter on the Principles of Judgment [After Death]

It is necessary to believe in compensation for the slaughtered animal. Know that the True One (may He be exalted) is all-wise, and does nothing futile (al-^^^^02bfabath). He (may He be praised and exalted) is just, and does nothing repugnant (al-qabīḥ). One cannot attribute to Him any kind of oppression or injustice, as is demonstrated by reason (al-^^^^02bfaql) and the Law (al-shar^^^^02bf).

Reason determines that inflicting harm is repugnant, unless it is justified by some additional rational factor. There are four factors by which a harm can be rationally justified. If a harm does not possess1 one of these, it becomes unjust, and injustice is repugnant.
1. The first factor is if the harm is deserved—for example, when we punish a criminal according to his crime.

2. The second factor is [if that] harm prevents a greater [harm]—for example, when we perform bloodletting by opening a vein, cupping, and scarifying, or when we amputate the finger of a person who has been stung, so that the venom does not spread to the rest of the body.
3. The third factor is if the harm is defensive, deterring one who intends to harm us in order to prevent injury to us.

4. The fourth factor is if the harm procures some benefit, such as when we weary ourselves, toiling in order to make a profit; or when we discipline our children so that they may benefit from what they learn, in both religious and worldly matters.

The kind of harm suffered by the animal by being slaughtered cannot be deserved by it, for the very cause of “deserving” is absent, since the animal is not bound by any obligations. Nor can it be for the sake of preventing some greater harm, for there is no harm greater than that of slaughter. Nor can it be defensive, for the animal poses us no threat that we should have to prevent it from carrying out.

Only the final factor remains, namely, harm for the sake of procuring some benefit. We must therefore believe that the True One (may He be praised and exalted) has afflicted [the animal] with this harm as a prelude to the compensation for the pain [that it suffers], as required by His justice (may He be praised and exalted). The Lord is righteous in all His ways, and faithful in all His works (Psalms 145:17).

For this purpose, we are not required to know how God will compensate [the animal for its suffering], but we are required to believe that the slaughtered animal will receive compensation for the pain caused to it by its being slaughtered, negating any oppression or injustice [on the part of God], affirming His justice (may He be praised and exalted), as necessitated by His wisdom (may He be praised and exalted).

p.i: May His name be blessed and His praise continue forever!
Amen, Neṣaḥ, Selah, and Peace upon Israel. Amen.

book.p: Thus conclude The Regulations of Slaughter
by our teacher and master, the aforementioned
Israel the Judge (may he rest in Eden).

p.i: What Must Be Removed from the Meat
After Slaughtering

book.p: We must now mention what applies to the meat, in the absence of which it would be impermissible to eat it after slaughtering. That is, it must be cleaned of three things: blood, fats, and the sciatic nerve. Scripture states, You shall not eat any fat or any blood (Leviticus 3:17); and, Therefore, the children of Israel shall not eat the sciatic nerve… (Genesis 32:33).

There are three things that are inaccessible until after the act of slaughtering. The first [of them], fat, is specified by name in the [Biblical] text. Concerning blood, He did not only command [us] once, but urging great caution, emphasized [the prohibition multiple times], But make sure that you do not eat the blood (Deuteronomy 12:23); it is the blood, as life, that makes atonement (Leviticus 17:11).

This is the fat that should be removed: the fat of the fat-tail; the fat that covers the circulatory system and stomach; the fat that adheres to the stomach itself; the kidneys and their fat, from the borderline between them and the intestine (this is the blood vessel and its extremity below and above, and from the upper part of the underskin to the place of excretion). The appendix of the liver and the two sinews (one on each side) must also be removed, as well as the tissue that is on the meat of the shoulders along with their fat, and the fat-tail up to the end of the coccyx.

The second matter is the blood: one must search for [the animal's] veins. The first are in the neck, where there are four: two, [one] on either side; and two in the middle. Next, the cranial membrane, and two veins from the ear to the eye; each of them are connected. There are eight in the tongue and the interior of the mouth on each side: four are embedded between the skin and the meat, two on each side of the interior of the mouth, and there are four on the sides of the tongue. Under the peritoneum are two veins that adhere to the thorax from beneath. There is a vein in each arm that is connected at the joint, and a vein between each rib. There is a white peritoneum in the hollows of the flanks, two circulatory veins, and the two veins of the heart, and five veins sunk beneath the location of each of the forbidden sinews. There are two roots and their membrane, and a vein in each specified part (?).2 These are all of the blood vessels.

The third matter is the sciatic nerve: one must cut into it from the surface of the thigh, following its seventeen branches to where it ends and emerges from the socket and knob (for they are its point of origin), along with the bones at the head of the neck, which are in the hind. One must clean the spine of the lower back, clear out its [vertebral] cavities, and extract its veins. One must cut into the sides of the trotters, and remove their veins. One must cut into each trotter and extract its veins.
Similarly, in poultry, there are four veins in the neck, and four veins in the wings. The two sciatic veins connect to the feet, and the seminal veins within the uropygium.

After all this, one should soak the meat, then salt it and remove it, soaking it up until the salt becomes saturated. Then one should rinse it no less than three times, before tossing it into a pot or roasting it, for there remains no further impediment to eating it.

p.i: Peace upon all Israel.
It is complete, by the help of God, may He be exalted.
Amen, Neṣaḥ, Selah.
